sentences: Crowds of people have poured out onto a frozen river.
This is Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters, painted around 1608 by the Dutch artist Hendrick Avercamp.
Avercamp lays the scene out as if we were looking down from a high vantage point.
That is why hundreds of figures fit into a single view.
People close to us are large and sharp, while those farther off grow small and pale in the misty air.
Avercamp was born in Amsterdam in 1585 and spent most of his life in the small town of Kampen.
He could not speak and was probably deaf as well, and people called him the Mute of Kampen.
Perhaps that is why his pictures seem to listen so carefully with the eyes.
He lived during the Little Ice Age, a long stretch of colder winters across northern Europe.
The winter of 1607 to 1608 was especially severe, and this painting dates from just that time.
Avercamp is counted as the first Dutch painter to specialise in scenes of snow and ice.
Now wander across the ice.
You can find people who skate, pull sledges, and hit a ball with long sticks in an early game called kolf.
Most of them are out for fun, but some are working, because the frozen river was also a place to earn a living.
Look at the lower left corner.
A dog and a few crows have gathered around a horse that froze to death.
In the middle of all this fun, Avercamp quietly reminds us how harsh the winter really was.
It is a detail many viewers miss at first.
In the foreground, fishermen struggle to free a sailboat trapped in the ice.
Farther back, a boat mounted on runners glides away like a sledge.
In winter the river became both a road and a town square.
Everyone in the picture is moving, talking, falling or working.
Look closely at the wall of the hut at lower right.
Avercamp signed the painting there, as if his name were graffiti scratched into the wood.
It is a small joke, and a nice reward for anyone who takes the time to search the picture like a puzzle.
In winter Avercamp went outdoors and made tiny, careful sketches of people from life.
He then seems to have moved those figures into his paintings back in the studio.
That is why each little person feels so alive, with a real posture and a real reason to be there.
The Rijksmuseum bought the painting in 1897 with help from the Rembrandt Association, a society that supports Dutch museums.
Today it hangs in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, where crowds of real visitors gather in front of the painted crowd.
Step back and look at the whole panel again.
Choose one person among the hundreds, someone who catches your eye, and imagine the day they are having on this frozen river.
